opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core problem we were trying to solve is that benchmarks saturate really quickly, and they're all on different scales. You get a model that scores 40% on one benchmark and 70% on another, and it's very hard to say what that actually means, or to compare progress across different kinds of tasks or across time. Once a benchmark hits 90-something percent, it just stops telling you anything.

So we wanted a metric that's grounded in something intuitive and that doesn't have a ceiling built into it. Human completion time turned out to be a pretty natural choice. We take a diverse set of tasks, mostly software engineering and research-style tasks, everything from things that take a skilled person a few seconds up to things that take many hours. We have actual human experts do them and measure how long they take. Then we look at how AI agents perform as a function of that human time. What you see is a fairly clean relationship: models are very reliable on short tasks, and their success rate drops off as tasks get longer. So you can fit a curve and ask, at what task length does this model succeed about 50% of the time? That's the "time horizon."

What's nice about it is that it puts very different tasks on a single axis that people can reason about. Saying a model can do tasks that take a human expert about an hour is much more meaningful to most people, and to policymakers, than saying it got some score on some benchmark. It also lets you plot models from GPT-2 through current frontier systems on the same scale, which you really can't do with most benchmarks because the older models score zero and the newer ones max it out. When we did that, we saw this surprisingly steady exponential trend, with the time horizon doubling roughly every seven months, and maybe faster more recently.

I want to be clear about the caveats, though. Human time is a proxy. It isn't a perfect measure of difficulty. Some tasks take humans a long time for boring reasons, like waiting on things or typing a lot, and some short tasks are conceptually hard. Our tasks are also cleaner and better specified than a lot of real-world work, which tends to be messy, underspecified, and full of context you have to pick up. So there's a real question about how well the numbers transfer to real deployment, and we've done some work looking at "messiness" factors for exactly that reason. But as a unifying metric that tracks something we actually care about, which is how much meaningful, autonomous work these systems can do, it's held up better than I expected.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks use different scales and cover different kinds of tasks, making progress hard to compare across tasks and over time.

r002.rationale: It describes timing human experts on tasks and using human completion time as a proxy for task difficulty, while noting the proxy has limitations.

r003.rationale: It says human time puts different tasks on a single axis and allows models from GPT-2 through current frontier systems to be compared on the same scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the motivation really came out of a frustration with how we were talking about AI capabilities. Every benchmark has its own scale, right? You get a number like 85 percent on MMLU or whatever, and then the benchmark saturates and you move to the next one, and there's no way to compare across them. You can't put GPT-2 and a current model on the same axis, because the things we tested GPT-2 on are just totally irrelevant to what we test models on now. So the question was, is there some underlying quantity that's actually continuous over the whole history of the field?

And the thing we landed on is: how long does this task take a human expert? That's a property of the task, not of the model, and it doesn't saturate. A task that takes a skilled person two minutes and a task that takes them two weeks are both just points on the same line. So you can take a model, give it a big spread of tasks with known human completion times, and ask: at what task length does this model succeed about half the time? That gives you a single number, a time horizon, and you can track it across years and across very different model generations.

The other reason I like it is that it's actually meaningful to people outside the field. If I tell you a model scores 60 percent on some benchmark, you don't know what to do with that. If I tell you it can reliably do things that take a software engineer an hour, but not things that take a day, that's an intuition you can immediately reason about. It connects directly to the question people actually care about, which is: what can this thing do that would otherwise take a person's time?

Now, it's definitely not perfect. Human time is a noisy proxy for difficulty. There are tasks that are fast for people and brutal for models, and vice versa, so the measure is best thought of as a rough, aggregate thing rather than something that tells you about any particular task. And you have to be careful about what population of humans you're baselining against, and what the task distribution looks like, because that can shift the number a lot. But as a way of getting a long-run, cross-era trend line, I haven't seen anything that works nearly as well.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks use different scales and test different tasks over time, making results difficult to compare across benchmarks and model generations.

r002.rationale: It proposes how long a human expert takes to complete a task as a property of that task and a measure of its difficulty.

r003.rationale: It describes human completion time as a shared line for tasks of different durations, enabling model comparisons across years and generations.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to put very different tasks on a common scale. If you measure progress by accuracy on a benchmark, it’s hard to compare that with accuracy on another benchmark: the tasks might require very different amounts of work. Human completion time gives us a more interpretable question: how much work could a person do in the time represented by the tasks an AI can solve?

It also helps distinguish systems that can answer short questions from systems that can carry out longer, more involved tasks. Those might look similarly impressive on a conventional benchmark, but they have quite different implications for what you can delegate.

It’s an imperfect measure, of course. Something that takes a human a long time isn’t necessarily hard for an AI, and you have to specify which humans you’re measuring and what level of reliability you require. But it’s a useful common yardstick for tracking the scope of work these systems can handle.

r001.rationale: It says benchmark tasks can require very different amounts of work, making their accuracy scores hard to compare.

r002.rationale: It mentions human completion time and notes that the measured person matters, but does not clearly identify task-appropriate expertise or say that completion time serves as a proxy for task difficulty.

r003.rationale: It presents human completion time as a common scale for comparing very different tasks and as a yardstick for tracking the scope of work AI systems can handle.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that human time gives us a common scale for tasks that otherwise look very different. If a model solves a math problem, writes a program, or answers a biology question, the scores on those benchmarks aren’t directly comparable. But we can ask: how long would a person with the relevant expertise take to do each of those things?

That helps distinguish getting better at lots of short questions from being able to carry out longer, more involved work. Those can look similar if you only report accuracy, but they have very different implications for what you can delegate to a model.

Of course, time isn’t a perfect measure of difficulty. Something that takes a human hours might be straightforward for a computer, and something we do almost instantly might be very hard for a model. You also have to specify which humans you’re measuring and what tools they have. So I’d treat it as a useful common yardstick, rather than a complete measure of intelligence.

r001.rationale: It says math, programming, and biology benchmarks produce scores that are not directly comparable because the tasks differ.

r002.rationale: It proposes asking how long a person with relevant expertise would take to complete each task.

r003.rationale: It describes human time as a common scale for comparing model performance across different task types and benchmarks.
